slides: The square. It's a shape almost all of us know, so let's go over its properties.

slides.say: All four sides of a square are equal, and all four angles are ninety degrees.
at: sides of a square are equal

slides.say: If the square is turned on the page, it's still a square. What decides is what the question says, not how the figure is drawn.
Now the diagonals of the square. First, they're equal to each other.
They also cut each other in half. So all four halves are equal: this one, this one, this one and this one.
at: They also cut each other in half

slides.say: They're perpendicular to each other: they meet at ninety degrees.
And they cut the square's angles in half. Each ninety splits into forty-five and forty-five, in every corner.
at: And they cut the square's angles in half

slides.say: Look at one of the four small triangles. Its angle in the middle is ninety degrees, because the diagonals are perpendicular. And its two legs are equal, because they're halves of equal diagonals. That's a silver triangle, forty-five, forty-five, ninety. So the square is made of four silver triangles.
at: Look at one of the four

slides.say: It's also made of two silver triangles, depending on how we look. Take half the square, cut along one diagonal. It has a ninety-degree angle and two equal legs, the sides of the square. And we can keep cutting. Draw a line from the right angle at B to the middle of the diagonal. That cuts the half square into two smaller silver triangles, and we can cut each of them again in the same way.

In a silver triangle, the hypotenuse is a leg times root two. In the half square, the hypotenuse is the diagonal, so the diagonal is the side times root two. A side of five gives a diagonal of five root two, and a side of seven gives seven root two.
at: the diagonal is the side times

slides.say: The area of a square is its side, squared. That's actually where the word squared comes from. If the side is a, the area is a squared.

Say each little square here is one square centimeter. Count the side: one, two, three, four, five, six. The side is six, so the area is six squared, thirty-six. And really, there are thirty-six little squares.
Another example: a side of nine gives nine squared, which is eighty-one square centimeters.

There's another way to find the area of a square. It's less known and less used: with the diagonals. Multiply the diagonals and divide by two. The two diagonals are equal, so it's the diagonal squared, over two.
Why does it work? Say the whole diagonal, from A to C, is twelve. Then half of it is six. The other diagonal is also twelve, so its halves are six too.
Look at one small triangle. Its legs are two halves, six and six, and they're perpendicular. So its area is six times six over two. Six times six is thirty-six, and half of thirty-six is eighteen.
The square is four of these triangles. Four times eighteen is seventy-two.

Now let's check the formula, the diagonal squared over two. Twelve squared over two is a hundred forty-four over two, and that's also seventy-two. Every square has these four equal triangles, and a longer or shorter diagonal doesn't change that split. So the formula works for every square.
Let's check one more: a diagonal of ten. Ten squared is a hundred, and a hundred over two is fifty.
One more fact about area, and it's true for every shape. Double the side of a square, from three to six.
The area doesn't double. It goes from nine to thirty-six, four times as much. Count the little squares: every row is twice as long, and there are twice as many rows. Two times two is four.
So when every length is multiplied by some number k, the area is multiplied by k squared. For example, if every length is three times as long, the area is nine times as big.

Careful, this works only when all the lengths grow. For a rectangle, if we double its length but keep its width the same, the area only doubles. Three by three is nine, and six by three is eighteen. Both sides must double for the area to become four times as big.
That's the square, the simplest and the most perfect quadrilateral. All the properties we just checked hold for a square.
at: All the properties we just checked
